Here is the breakdown of why:

### 1. The Altitude (The "Height" Factor)
An altitude of **5.272 degrees** is quite low. For context, if you hold your arm out straight in front of you, the Moon is only about the width of your fist above the horizon. Because it is so low, it will be partially obscured by local geography (buildings, trees, or hills) depending on exactly where you are standing in Edinburgh. ### 2. The Azimuth (The "Direction" Factor)
An azimuth of **59.687 degrees** puts the Moon in the East-North-East. Since you are in Edinburgh, you should look toward the direction of the Firth of Forth (if you are facing east/northeast toward the water).

### 3. The Sky Brightness (The "Contrast" Factor)
You mentioned the sky is in **nautical twilight**. This is the most favorable part of your data. Nautical twilight means the sun is far enough below the horizon that the sky is dark enough for navigation, but there is still some residual light. 
*   **The Good News:** Because the Moon is **88.2% illuminated** (a Waxing Gibbous), it is very bright. It will stand out significantly against the darkening sky.
*   **The Challenge:** Because it is so low, "atmospheric extinction" occurs. The Moon’s light has to travel through a much thicker layer of the Earth's atmosphere at that angle, which can make it look slightly dimmer, more orange/yellow, and potentially "fuzzy" compared to when it is high in the sky.

### 4. Visibility Verdict
Since you have "normal unaided eyesight" and the sky is clear:
*   **If you have a clear line of sight:** You will definitely see it. It will be a bright, prominent object.
*   **If there are trees or buildings:** You might struggle to see it because it is so close to the horizon line.

**Pro-tip for spotting it:** Don't look directly at the horizon line where the ground meets the sky. Instead, look slightly *above* the horizon toward the East-North-East. Because it is so low, your eyes might naturally "filter out" something that is sitting right on the edge of the earth.
